{"id": "2:114/q11", "question": "What does the fearful-entry clause mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it states rightful reverence, predicts reversal of power, or commands exclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q11/p1", "position": "Christians or Romans enter Jerusalem secretly fearing beating, execution or jizya.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and others describe disguise, severe beating, death or poll tax after the Muslim rebuilding. Al-Rāzī objects that Christians later held Jerusalem for more than a century; al-Ālūsī says one period suffices for the promise."}, {"id": "2:114/q11/p2", "position": "It predicts Muslim victory, recovery of mosques and their fearful entry.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj links 9:33; al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite the conquest, ban on polytheist pilgrimage and expulsion. Al-Ālūsī says Crusader control later does not negate a promise fulfilled once. Abū Ḥayyān objects that mā kāna lahum expresses propriety, not plain prediction."}, {"id": "2:114/q11/p3", "position": "The declarative form commands Muslims to bar or expel the offenders.", "reasons": "Explanations compare 33:53; some demand jihad until fearful entry, others forbid enabling access. Ibn Kathīr specifies truce and jizya. Abū Ḥayyān finds this strained."}, {"id": "2:114/q11/p4", "position": "They ought to fear believers' punishment and must not seize mosques.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī say oppression prevented this rightful arrangement; al-Ālūsī reads lām as entitlement violated."}, {"id": "2:114/q11/p5", "position": "The offenders ought to enter reverently, fearing God and His punishment.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers the mosque's dignity as the direct force of mā kāna lahum and rejects a simple future prediction and command. Al-Ālūsī says the lām marks fitting entitlement; Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects this because the demonstrative makes the condition a consequence of offense."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q12", "question": "What access to mosques may non-Muslims have?", "turns_on": "The sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, scope of 9:28, reports of actual entry, and whether 2:114 proves exclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q12/p1", "position": "They may enter no mosque, apart from reported necessity or judicial exceptions.", "reasons": "Mālik invokes 9:28 and purification from impurity. Al-Jubbāʾī allows a litigant brief fearful entry to ordinary mosques; Abū ʿAlī gives judicial authority. Al-Qurṭubī reads fear as expulsion or discipline."}, {"id": "2:114/q12/p2", "position": "The Sacred Mosque is barred to them; ordinary mosques are distinguished.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī cites 9:28, 22:26, 9:17–18 and 2:114, with the sanctuary's special sanctity. Al-Rāzī rejects narrowing 9:28 to pilgrimage and notes 17:1 can use Sacred Mosque for the whole sanctuary."}, {"id": "2:114/q12/p3", "position": "They may enter mosques generally.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥanīfa cites this verse, lodging of the Thaqīf delegation and sanctuary safety. Al-Rāzī says the historical reports predate 9:28 and rejects analogy from ordinary mosques to the Sacred Mosque."}, {"id": "2:114/q12/p4", "position": "The verse itself does not settle the legal entry rule.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it points toward but does not explicitly prohibit entry; Abū Ḥayyān says his reverence reading cannot prove exclusion or fearful entry permission. Asad and Kuran Yolu cite the Christian Najrān delegation worshipping in the Prophet's mosque."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q13", "question": "What does khizy mean and what is their worldly disgrace?", "turns_on": "Whether disgrace takes the form of jizya, war losses, exclusion, conquests, or a wider humiliation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q13/p1", "position": "Belligerents face killing or captivity; protected non-Muslims pay jizya in humiliation.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Zajjāj and many others distinguish the two legal statuses. Al-Ṭabarī includes both in worldly abasement."}, {"id": "2:114/q13/p2", "position": "Their cities will be conquered, especially Constantinople, Rome and Amorium.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Kalbī list the cities; al-Suddī and others connect conquest to the Mahdī, killing and captivity. Al-Farrāʾ places it at the end of time, while Jishumī rejects that as against the apparent sense. Elmalılı treats Constantinople's later fall as a fulfilled prophecy."}, {"id": "2:114/q13/p3", "position": "Khizy is disgrace or abasement, broadly covering punitive loss of power.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī include killing, captivity and jizya; Ibn Kathīr says the sense exceeds specific glosses. Elmalılı describes loss of state and strength. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies Badr deaths, captivity and flight at the conquest."}, {"id": "2:114/q13/p4", "position": "For Quraysh it is defeat, killing, captivity and expulsion at the conquest.", "reasons": "This reading distinguishes those who died unbelievers for afterlife punishment; al-Ālūsī adds destroyed idols and leaders' deaths."}, {"id": "2:114/q13/p5", "position": "Their disgrace is being excluded from mosques or the Sacred Mosque.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and others take denied entry as public abasement; Ibn Kathīr frames expulsion as repayment for barring believers."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q14", "question": "What is the great punishment in the hereafter, and why is it great?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q14/p1", "position": "It is Hellfire, commensurate with unbelief and grave wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and many others identify Hell; al-Zajjāj, al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī link greatness to the opening accusation. Abū Ḥayyān says its degree distinguishes unbelievers from believers and its fire mirrors their demolition; Ibn Kathīr cites desecration with idols and naked circumambulation."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q15", "question": "How does this verse connect with its neighbors and other verses?", "turns_on": "The proposed historical addressee and how the passage turns to 2:115.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q15/p1", "position": "It follows the rebuke of Jews and Christians by exposing Christian offenses.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 2:113 and 2:116; al-Rāzī says Christian destruction contradicts their Paradise claim; al-Ālūsī makes this the first occasion's link."}, {"id": "2:114/q15/p2", "position": "It turns from Jews and Christians to Arab polytheists with analogous conduct.", "reasons": "Jishumī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀshūr find the previous mention of those without knowledge or a digression. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the qibla dispute: exclusion from the sanctuary was graver than facing another direction."}, {"id": "2:114/q15/p3", "position": "The passage is linked to other mosque and worship verses.", "reasons": "The sources cite 9:17–18 on mosque maintenance, 9:28 on barring polytheists, 22:40 on protection of all houses of worship and 72:18 on mosques belonging to God."}, {"id": "2:114/q15/p4", "position": "Verse 2:115 consoles those denied Jerusalem or a mosque: east and west belong to God.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhān's explanation appears in al-Burhān and al-Itqān."}, {"id": "2:114/q15/p5", "position": "The next statement about God taking a son connects to the mosque-preventer passage.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī uses the Syrian codex reading of Ibn ʿĀmir without the waw before qālū to mark the connection."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q16", "question": "What inward or spiritual analogy do the sources draw?", "turns_on": "Whether inward allusion is legitimate and whether it replaces the outward meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q16/p1", "position": "Mosques may analogize hearts, souls, spirits and inner secrets; ruin is desire and veiling.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī distinguishes ruined homes of worship, gnosis, love and witnessing. Qāshānī and al-Ālūsī read divine names manifesting according to the heart, desire and fanaticism clouding it, humbled entry, worldly exposure and afterlife veiling. Ibn ʿĀshūr frames this as analogy, not a substitute exegesis; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it as unsupported."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q17", "question": "What does this verse teach about honoring and maintaining worship places?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q17/p1", "position": "Preventing worship is grave; maintaining worship places includes use, repair and protecting worshippers.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 72:18, 9:18, 24:36 and reports on mosque building, attendance and prayer rewards. Al-Qurṭubī stresses prayer's merit, mosque public status and protection against demolition. Asad and Kuran Yolu extend respect to churches and synagogues per 22:40."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q18", "question": "What conduct and activities in mosques do the cited reports discuss?", "turns_on": "Different rulings on entry prayer, sleeping, transactions, adjudication and upkeep.", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q18/p1", "position": "Mosques are for prayer, remembrance, cleanliness and dignified use.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī collects reports against trade, poetry, lost-property calls, spitting and odors; records greetings, sleeping, reclining, building without distracting decoration, and differences over greeting prayer and adjudication. The Bedouin urination report requires cleaning with water and teaching the mosque's purpose."}]}
{"id": "2:114/q19", "question": "What other cited reports or scholarly discussions accompany the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:114/q19/p1", "position": "Ancillary reports and methodological discussions appear alongside the exegesis.", "reasons": "The Musnad report describes ʿAlī's ablution and his ranking of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. Ibn al-Jawzī surveys masjid referents elsewhere. Bursevī cites a Mathnawī poem about confusing shadow and source. Rifāʿī surveys the controversy over Khalafallāh, symbolic Qurʾānic narrative, and responses from al-Khūlī, Muḥammad ʿAbduh and critics. {"id": "2:142/q01", "question": "What does the future form of 'will say' indicate?", "turns_on": "Whether the objection was foretold before it arose or was already being repeated.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q01/p1", "position": "It predicts an objection before it occurs.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai and Alusi say forewarning cushions its impact, prepares an answer and confirms prophecy when fulfilled; Ibn Ashur says it forestalls a claim that criticism caused the change. Jishumi calls it consolation and a sign. Bursevi says readiness lessens shock; Alusi reports an alternative that advance notice marks foolishness but replies that the later exchange would show this too."}, {"id": "2:142/q01/p2", "position": "It marks persistence or recurrence of an objection already voiced.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Qaffal, Abu Hayyan, Burhan, Suyuti and Study Quran cite reports of earlier speech; Abu Hayyan favors this chronology from al-Bara and resists making sin itself past-tense. Ibn Hisham says the imperfect carries continuity while sin remains future."}, {"id": "2:142/q01/p3", "position": "The future particle assures fulfillment of the prediction.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari makes sin strengthen the promised event; Suyuti calls this confirmation of a promise or threat. Tibī's equation with inna in negative speech is rejected because it shifts emphasis from promise to event."}, {"id": "2:142/q01/p4", "position": "Sin marks the nearer future, compared with sawfa.", "reasons": "Grammarians cited in Burhan say sawfa is more delayed; Suyuti says sin attaches to an affirmative ungoverned imperfect and expands time."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q02", "question": "How is the plural 'the foolish' formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q02/p1", "position": "Sufahāʾ is the plural of safīh.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit says the singular is one who lightly rushes toward what should be avoided."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q03", "question": "What does 'the foolish' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names ordinary intellectual lightness or a sharper moral fault.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q03/p1", "position": "People of light or defective judgment, hence ignorant or foolish.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Nahhas give its plural morphology; Mawardi compares thin cloth and a quick spear; Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Jawzi cite loose weave, wind and Dhu al-Rumma's poetry; Razi says religious error is most harmful; Biqai says acting without evidence; Kuranyolu adds crude or aggressive usage."}, {"id": "2:142/q03/p2", "position": "A knowingly slanderous liar.", "reasons": "Al-Muarrij says the safih deliberately contradicts known truth."}, {"id": "2:142/q03/p3", "position": "An extremely unjust and ignorant person.", "reasons": "Qutrub's gloss combines moral wrongdoing and ignorance."}, {"id": "2:142/q03/p4", "position": "In other Qur'anic usage it can denote dependents or self-ruin.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi reports women and children in 4:5 and ruin of oneself in 2:130; this distinguishes other contexts from 2:142."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q04", "question": "Who are the foolish speakers?", "turns_on": "Reports name Jews, Meccan polytheists, hypocrites, combinations, or an unrestricted set.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q04/p1", "position": "Jews, especially Medina's Jews or Jewish scholars.", "reasons": "Mujahid, al-Bara, Ibn Abbas and others name Jews; Tabari describes rejection of an Arab messenger. Ibn Abbas names Rifa'a, Qardam, Ka'b al-Ashraf and other leaders; their opposition to abandoning Jerusalem and to abrogation explains the objection. Kuranyolu favors this historical setting."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p2", "position": "Hypocrites.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi and others say they mocked the change as arbitrary; Razi and Elmalili cite the earlier designation of hypocrites as fools in 2:13. Elmalili prefers this link."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p3", "position": "Meccan polytheists or Quraysh.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Hasan, Zajjaj and others report their taunt that Muhammad returned to his ancestral qibla and would return to their religion; Ibn Ashur's contextual reading specifically expects this objection before the Kaaba command."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p4", "position": "All three groups, or all unbelieving objectors.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baydawi, Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Jishumi and Tabatabai combine groups; Razi and Alusi argue the definite plural is general, while Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi include anyone who asked. Qadi observes that the text only proves some group spoke, without requiring universality."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p5", "position": "Jews and hypocrites.", "reasons": "Tabari names both; Ibn Atiyya reports al-Suddi's pairing, and Elmalili allows both."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p6", "position": "Jews and Meccan polytheists.", "reasons": "Wahidi Wajiz, Baghawi and Tabatabai include these two groups."}, {"id": "2:142/q04/p7", "position": "People of the Book, possibly including polytheists.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim names the People of the Book while allowing others; Ibn Ishaq's al-Bara report says People of the Book."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q05", "question": "Why say 'among people'?", "turns_on": "Whether it chiefly qualifies human speakers, compares them with humanity, or restricts a subset.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q05/p1", "position": "It specifies human fools because foolishness can be ascribed to things and animals.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Samin cite cloth, spears and animals; Samin calls it a circumstantial phrase governed by sayaqūl, and Tabrisi likewise gives circumstantial syntax."}, {"id": "2:142/q05/p2", "position": "It marks comparison with humanity generally and heightens their disgrace.", "reasons": "Alusi parses an accusative circumstantial phrase with generic al-nas and prefers this; Biqai says it broadens censure to all who side with them."}, {"id": "2:142/q05/p3", "position": "It specifies the worst among unbelievers, rather than every member.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this restricted reading of al-nas and rejects it in favor of generic humanity."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q06", "question": "What does 'what turned them' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the question asks what caused a turn, or names the agent and its rhetorical force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q06/p1", "position": "What diverted or redirected them from the former direction.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Tabari, Zajjaj, Ata and others gloss turning away; Jishumi contrasts turning away with toward; Tabrisi traces walī to succession without gap; Razi cites 8:16; Tabatabai describes putting a place before the face or turning one's back."}, {"id": "2:142/q06/p2", "position": "Who caused them to turn away?", "reasons": "Thalabi and Kashshaf phrase mā as asking the agent; Bursevi calls it emphatic and Biqai sees a contemptuous choice of mā instead of man."}, {"id": "2:142/q06/p3", "position": "The question expresses mockery or astonishment.", "reasons": "Razi and Alusi call it reproachful; Suyuti permits either astonishment or a genuine inquiry; Qushayri says objectors doubt that the first direction was true if later abandoned."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q07", "question": "How is 'what turned them' parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q07/p1", "position": "Mā is an interrogative subject, wallāhum its predicate, and ʿan qiblatihim depends on the verb.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Tabrisi and Samin agree on the subject-predicate construction and complement."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q08", "question": "Whom do the pronouns in 'turned them' and 'their qibla' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronouns refer to Muslims or the critics and their forebears.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q08/p1", "position": "The Prophet and believers.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says it is called theirs because they faced it long; Wahidi Basit prefers the majority view. Tabatabai says attributing it to Muslims heightens the objection."}, {"id": "2:142/q08/p2", "position": "The critics and their inherited directions or ancestral qibla.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim and Abu Hayyan allow critics' Jewish and Christian directions; Ata via Ibn Abbas takes the ancestors Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and tribes as the pronoun's referent."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q09", "question": "What does 'qibla' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q09/p1", "position": "The posture or direction of facing, conventionally the place faced in prayer.", "reasons": "Tabari notes faʿla like jalsa and qaʿda; Wahidi, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Baydawi, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalili derive it from facing. Razi cites Qutrub's idiom of direction/refuge, reciprocity between two who face, and a poetic use. Harali calls it what is opposite the face."}, {"id": "2:142/q09/p2", "position": "The Kaaba is the Muslims' qibla as a term of worship.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Kuranyolu explicitly identify the Kaaba as the canonical prayer direction and say facing it is a condition of valid prayer."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q10", "question": "What is the 'qibla they had been on'?", "turns_on": "The main reports identify Jerusalem, while alternatives identify the Kaaba or critics' directions.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q10/p1", "position": "Jerusalem, the former Muslim prayer direction.", "reasons": "Tabari, Rabi, Ata, Wahidi and many later writers identify Jerusalem; Wahidi Basit prefers this as the exegetical majority and Razi accepts transmitted reports over Abu Muslim's hypothetical alternative. It could be called the Rock or Syrian direction."}, {"id": "2:142/q10/p2", "position": "The Kaaba, originally faced before a move to Jerusalem.", "reasons": "Some cited by Abu Hayyan say the Meccans reproached the Prophet for leaving Abraham's qibla. Ibn Ashur prefers this reading for the local sequence of Abraham and the House; Biqai says leaving the former direction unnamed can evoke the Kaaba."}, {"id": "2:142/q10/p3", "position": "The critics' own Jewish and Christian directions.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim s
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

uggests this without reports; Jishumi says Jews and Christians faced west and east respectively, and Razi says their established directions make facing the Kaaba surprising. Abu Hayyan records this pronoun reading."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q11", "question": "What does 'they had been on it' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q11/p1", "position": "It stresses sustained attachment and sharpens the rebuke.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls ʿalā figurative as if bearing the orientation; Samin supplies an omitted word such as orientation or belief; Alusi says the relative clause after 'their' intensifies criticism."}, {"id": "2:142/q11/p2", "position": "On one account the expression is understood as the qibla now being faced.", "reasons": "Qurtubi records the interpretation of kunt ʿalayhā as anta ʿalayhā in an account of abrogation twice."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q12", "question": "Why were opponents troubled by the change?", "turns_on": "The notes give several motives, sometimes assigned to different groups.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q12/p1", "position": "Polytheists claimed a return to the ancestral direction vindicated their religion.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Hasan, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya and others report the taunt that longing for birthplace would lead back to their religion. Jishumi notes this was to make their own practice appear true."}, {"id": "2:142/q12/p2", "position": "Hypocrites mocked a seemingly arbitrary shift.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, Razi, Alusi and Kuranyolu depict cynicism or the claim that directions are equivalent and no rational reason distinguishes them."}, {"id": "2:142/q12/p3", "position": "Jews denied abrogation or feared loss of their religious distinction.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Nasafi, Tabatabai, Alusi and Ibn Ashur say Jerusalem's replacement affronted Jews; Tabatabai says they thought it honored by earlier prophets and doubted that God could change it."}, {"id": "2:142/q12/p4", "position": "Jews offered to believe if the Prophet returned, seeking to tempt him.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas names Jewish leaders; the offer is reported by Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya and others; Alusi suspects insincerity."}, {"id": "2:142/q12/p5", "position": "The critics' judgment was veiled by habitual belief or envy.", "reasons": "Qushayri says unbelievers object to each new affair; Qashani says restricted orientation and attachment to prior beliefs block recognition of comprehensive unity; Kuranyolu calls the roots ignorance and envy. Biqai says they spoke indirectly to followers after arguments failed."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q13", "question": "Why is the question phrased 'their qibla' rather than 'the Jews' qibla'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q13/p1", "position": "It preserves surprise and sharpens the challenge.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says explicitly naming the Jews' qibla would make the reason for departure obvious; Alusi says the additional clause about following it intensifies rebuke."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q14", "question": "Why is the former qibla left unnamed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q14/p1", "position": "The ambiguity can evoke both Jerusalem and the Kaaba.", "reasons": "Biqai says either way the critics fault God's command and expose desire."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q15", "question": "What force does the command 'Say' have here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q15/p1", "position": "It supplies a divine reply before or upon the objection.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi emphasize a ready answer that silences a challenge; Biqai notes the unaddressed qul contrasts with direct challenges in 2:80 and 2:111 because critics would not face believers openly."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q16", "question": "What are 'east and west' here?", "turns_on": "The pair may encompass every direction or evoke specific historical prayer directions.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q16/p1", "position": "The two horizons stand for all lands and directions.", "reasons": "Tabari describes the world between extremes of sunrise and sunset; Kashshaf and Nasafi take the lands, Biqai the horizons, and Tabatabai notes relative solar and stellar orientations."}, {"id": "2:142/q16/p2", "position": "The pair evokes eastward Christians and westward Jews.", "reasons": "Some shaykhs relate Jewish orientation to Moses and 28:44, Christian orientation to Mary and 19:16; Bursevi says they chose those directions by preference. Ibn Ashur reports and interprets this allusion."}, {"id": "2:142/q16/p3", "position": "East is the Kaaba from Medina and west is Jerusalem.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit reports this geographic gloss."}, {"id": "2:142/q16/p4", "position": "East is Jerusalem and west the Kaaba.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives the Kaaba as west of Jerusalem."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q17", "question": "What does God's ownership of east and west answer?", "turns_on": "Whether ownership itself suffices or direction changes should be explained by changing benefit.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q17/p1", "position": "No direction has intrinsic authority; God appoints whichever He wills and obedience is decisive.", "reasons": "Tabari, Zajjaj, Mawardi, Razi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Alusi, Tabatabai and Kuranyolu state sovereignty over all places. Tabatabai relates legislation to individual and collective perfection. Ibn Kathir links obedience to 2:177; Tabrisi rejects priority for prophets' Holy Land."}, {"id": "2:142/q17/p2", "position": "The change tracks wisdom or the benefit appropriate to a time.", "reasons": "Jishumi prefers changed benefit; Tabrisi says God sanctifies places for people's interests; Baydawi and Alusi make welfare the straightness of successive orientations."}, {"id": "2:142/q17/p3", "position": "God's knowledge and presence are not bounded by a direction.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites 6:3, 57:4 and 58:7 to say God knows and is present wherever worship is commanded; Qashani says the Real is in no direction though all directions relate to Him, citing 2:115."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q18", "question": "How is 'He guides whom He wills' understood?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance is indication, God's effective creation of knowledge, or a person's willing receptivity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q18/p1", "position": "God grants and directs guidance to whomever He wills.", "reasons": "Tabari applies it to believers receiving Abraham's qibla while others are left astray; Muqatil calls the destination Islam; Qushayri says divine light; Elmalili says foundational grace and prophethood precede human acquisition and cites 2:286."}, {"id": "2:142/q18/p2", "position": "Guidance is indication toward what benefits a person.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates yahdi with yadullu and calls indication the root sense; the Mu'tazila define it as directing servants to the best road to Paradise."}, {"id": "2:142/q18/p3", "position": "Guidance is God's creation of knowledge, beyond a general invitation.", "reasons": "Razi reports the Ash'ari objection: invitation and indication reach all accountable people, but this selective guidance and misguidance are divine acts."}, {"id": "2:142/q18/p4", "position": "God guides whoever wills to be guided.", "reasons": "Asad offers this alternate rendering of man yashaʾ."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q19", "question": "How does the verb of guidance govern its destination?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q19/p1", "position": "Hadā may take lām, ilā or no preposition; here it takes ilā.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan explicitly distinguishes these constructions."}]}

{"id": "2:142/q41", "question": "What stopping and beginning rules are illustrated near 'will say'?", "turns_on": "Stop taxonomies differ in scope.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q41/p1", "position": "An absolute stop can precede self-contained fresh speech.", "reasons": "Suyuti uses sayaqūlu al-sufahāʾ as an independent verb example; he lists questions, negations, conditions and omitted objects as other contexts but bars a stop between subject and predicate or condition and consequence."}, {"id": "2:142/q41/p2", "position": "Stops can be classified in eight grades.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports another scholar's complete, near-complete, deficient, near-deficient, good, near-good, ugly and near-ugly scheme."}, {"id": "2:142/q41/p3", "position": "Voluntary and forced stops are more defensible divisions.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari finds conventional categories unbounded and says complete speech permits a voluntary stop, while a truly complete stop lacks lexical or semantic tie to following text."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q42", "question": "What legal lesson about sincerity appears in nearby discussion?", "turns_on": "Reports distinguish devotional sacrifice from social celebration.", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q42/p1", "position": "Worship begun sincerely follows its initial intention, but display has no added merit.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites Tatarhaniyya on ostentatious prayer, a sage's pebbles-to-market simile, and a report that God accepts only sincere deeds."}, {"id": "2:142/q42/p2", "position": "Sacrifice devoted to other than God is forbidden.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites a report cursing such sacrifice and Nawawi's explanation of slaughter in another's name, such as an idol or Moses. Marwadhi applies this to slaughter honoring a ruler as devotion."}, {"id": "2:142/q42/p3", "position": "Slaughter celebrating a ruler's arrival can be permissible.", "reasons": "Rafi'i likens it to an aqiqah; Bursevi prefers a charitable interpretation of Muslims' acts to avoid charges of unbelief."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q43", "question": "What other descriptions of the Qur'an appear in related notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q43/p1", "position": "It is called mutashabih, ruh, majid and aziz for different qualities.", "reasons": "Suyuti says its parts resemble one another in truth and beauty, it gives hearts life, is noble, and cannot be rivaled."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q44", "question": "What did the qibla event teach believers about response to revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q44/p1", "position": "Successive commands test sincere obedience, and earlier worship is not lost.", "reasons": "Qatada says each command tests submission and 2:143 assures believers about prior prayers; Ibn Kathir says the immediate congregational turn demonstrates complete compliance and distinguishes followers."}, {"id": "2:142/q44/p2", "position": "It establishes a distinct communal emblem.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu links the straight path to Islam's qibla; Tabatabai says a shared direction has strong outward and inward effects; Study Quran's introduction identifies qibla as canonical prayer orientation."}]}
{"id": "2:142/q45", "question": "What does the verse announce and answer about the changed qibla?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:142/q45/p1", "position": "It addresses the turn to the Kaaba and rebuts objections through divine ownership and guidance.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit says the verse came for the changed direction; Ibn Abi Hatim reports Jewish doubt followed by God's reply; Elmalili connects the new direction to a new guided community."}]}
